Exploring LTSA spectral blocks

Source: vignettes/articles/spectral-blocks.Rmd
spectral-blocks.Rmd

LTSA uses ndim twice: once to build the local tangent spaces and again to choose how many global coordinates to return. Those choices can differ. A circle is locally one-dimensional, for example, but two coordinates show its closed path.

spectral_dim retains extra coordinates from the same LTSA operator. This article shows how to inspect them on a circle, COIL-20, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST.

Click any figure to open a larger version; click the enlarged image or press Escape to close it. Keyboard users can focus a figure and press Enter or Space.

Keep More Modes from the Same Operator

Given a data matrix X, request four low-frequency modes while keeping a two-dimensional local tangent model and a two-coordinate returned embedding:

fit <- flotsam::ltsa(
  X,
  ndim = 2,
  n_neighbors = 15,
  output = "result",
  spectral_dim = 4
)

dim(fit$embedding)                    # n by 2
dim(fit$spectral_embedding)           # n by 4
identical(
  fit$embedding,
  fit$spectral_embedding[, 1:2, drop = FALSE]
)
Control Changes B? Purpose
ndim yes Sets the local tangent rank and displayed prefix
spectral_dim no Retains extra nonconstant modes from the fixed operator
eig_k no Gives the eigensolver a numerical candidate span

Most users can leave eig_k at its default. When retaining an expanded block, a manual request must be at least spectral_dim + 2: one place for the known constant direction and another for the mode just beyond the retained block.

The displayed and retained boundaries have separate diagnostics:

fit$eigen$diagnostics$scaled_boundary_gap
fit$eigen$spectral$diagnostics$scaled_boundary_gap
fit$eigen$status
fit$eigen$spectral$status

A boundary gap compares the last included mode with the next one. A large gap isolates the chosen subspace. A small gap suggests interpreting the neighboring modes together and checking their geometry and support.

A Circle Needs a Spectral Pair

A circle has a one-dimensional tangent at every point. A single real-valued coordinate cannot follow the whole loop continuously, so the first two low-frequency modes work as a pair. Their signs and orientation can change between fits; treat the two-dimensional span as the stable unit.

The example uses exact neighbors and dense eigenanalysis, making the repeated pairs easy to see.

library(flotsam)
theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 721)[-721]
circle <- cbind(x = cos(theta), y = sin(theta))

circle_fit <- ltsa(
  circle,
  ndim = 1,
  n_neighbors = 9,
  nn_method = "exact",
  eig_method = "eig",
  eig_k = 8,
  output = "result",
  spectral_dim = 4
)

circle_fit$eigen$values
#> [1] 4.464673e-07
circle_fit$eigen$spectral$values
#> [1] 4.464673e-07 4.464673e-07 7.139639e-06 7.139639e-06
circle_fit$eigen$status
#> [1] "warning"
circle_fit$eigen$messages
#> [1] "Weak Ritz boundary gap after the selected block: 2.635e-18 < 1e-04."

The input circle, its one-dimensional LTSA display, the first two modes from the same operator, and the low spectrum. The mode pair follows the complete periodic progression.

Setting ndim = 2 would build a two-dimensional local tangent model. This fit instead keeps ndim = 1 and uses spectral_dim = 4: the first two retained modes reveal the global coordinate pair, while the next two expose its neighboring spectral context.

COIL-20: A Real Periodic Example

COIL-20 contains 72 views of each object as it rotates. One object traces a closed, locally one-dimensional curve through pixel space, so the circle example predicts a spectral pair.

At k = 7, mixing objects produces a disconnected neighbor graph, so we fit objects separately. Objects 4 and 1 were selected before embedding using a screen for connected graphs and good coverage of the pose sequence. Each fit uses standard LTSA with ndim = 1, exact neighbors, and four retained modes. The coordinates come from pixels; pose supplies the point colors and thumbnail labels.

COIL-20 object 4. Modes 1 and 2 form a pose-ordered orbit, with thumbnails placed in the same radial direction as their observations.
COIL-20 object 1. The path is more distorted and still follows the object’s rotation.

For objects 4 and 1, the gap after mode 2 is about 23 and 12 times larger, respectively, than the gap between modes 1 and 2. This is the spectral pattern expected from a mode pair. The second mode completes the rotational orbit already present in the fixed operator.

Check Whether a Mode Represents Many Observations

A low-energy mode can be dominated by a few observations. For a Euclidean-normalized coordinate vector v, the effective support fraction is

\frac{1}{n\sum_i v_i^4}.

This is the normalized participation ratio. It equals 1/n when one observation carries the mode, r/n when the energy is spread equally across exactly r observations, and 1 when it is spread equally across all observations. Here, a mode’s energy means its squared coordinate values, v^2:

effective_support_fraction <- function(v) {
  v <- v / sqrt(sum(v^2))
  1 / (length(v) * sum(v^4))
}

This scalar shows whether a coordinate is carried by many observations or only a few. The plots then reveal the variation organized by a broadly supported coordinate.

For a block of linearly independent coordinates, first orthonormalize its columns. Each observation’s block leverage is the sum of its squared entries across that basis. Divide those leverages by their sum to get influence fractions p, then compute 1 / (n * sum(p^2)):

block_support_fraction <- function(V) {
  Q <- qr.Q(qr(V))
  p <- rowSums(Q^2) / ncol(Q)
  1 / (nrow(Q) * sum(p^2))
}

This block support is unchanged by rotating or rescaling coordinates within the span. It does not establish where the span should end, so read it together with the boundary gap.

MNIST: Inspect a Neighboring Pair

The 7,877 MNIST digit-1 images illustrate what an extra coordinate can add to an existing display. Here we use Jacobi-normalized LTSA, with ndim = 2, k = 15, and four retained modes. The question is what to show from that fixed operator. The normalization article examines the separate decision to change the estimator.

The first pair forms a curved band; replacing mode 1 with mode 3 gives a loop with two branches. These plots show the full coordinate ranges, including the more distant points. Each panel has its own axes, with equal physical units on both axes.

Full-range normalized LTSA embeddings of MNIST digit 1. Modes 1 and 2 form a curved band; modes 2 and 3 form a loop with branches and distant points.

The first pair arranges handwriting by slant, curvature, stroke width, hooks, and serifed or branched forms. Its block support is 0.480, with a mode 2–3 boundary gap of 0.00201. To see the handwriting behind the shapes, expand the central views. Numbered thumbnails are chosen to cover that region; the plot titles report how many observations fall outside each frame.

MNIST: Modes 1 and 2 with Image Thumbnails
A closer view of normalized LTSA modes 1 and 2 for MNIST digit 1, with numbered thumbnails showing variation in handwriting.
MNIST: Modes 2 and 3 with Image Thumbnails
A closer view of normalized LTSA modes 2 and 3 for MNIST digit 1, with numbered thumbnails showing variation in handwriting.

Mode 3 is less broadly supported than modes 1 and 2. Across all four retained modes, block support falls to 0.0497, with a mode 4–5 gap of 0.00196. The additional coordinates therefore deserve more care than the first pair. Keeping them makes the complementary view available; it does not mean all four coordinates are equally useful.

MNIST low spectra and per-mode support. The normalized first pair has much broader support than its later modes; the ordinary fit is included for reference and is highly concentrated.

Fashion-MNIST: Extra Modes Can Stay Concentrated

Trousers, dresses, and bags provide a different reason to inspect a block: we want to know whether concentration is confined to the first two modes. Each class contains 7,000 images and uses one fixed approximate-neighbor graph. We fit standard LTSA with ndim = 2, k = 15, and twelve retained modes.

In all three first-pair displays, block support is close to the two-point benchmark 2 / 7000. The largest 1% of observations carry more than 99.98% of the displayed span’s leverage.

The ordinary two-dimensional LTSA displays for three Fashion-MNIST classes, shown at their full coordinate ranges. Orange points 1 and 2 are the two highest-leverage observations in each displayed span; the matching source images appear directly below each plot. Nearly all other images collapse near the origin.

The source images identify those extreme points as atypical striped or noisy records. They set the visible scale, while most garments are compressed together. The graphs are connected, the local patches have full rank, and the eigensolves converge, so we also inspect the extra modes.

Fashion-MNIST spectra through mode 13 and per-mode effective support through mode 12. Every retained mode is localized; separators mark the displayed and retained boundaries.

All 36 coordinates across the three classes remain near the single-point support limit, 1 / 7000. The twelve-coordinate block supports are also close to the corresponding 12 / 7000 benchmark.

For these fits, looking farther into the computed block does not reveal a broadly supported coordinate. The mode 12–13 gaps are weak, so this conclusion stops at the twelve modes inspected. To investigate changing the weighting of the estimator itself, see Jacobi-Normalized LTSA.

What to Carry into Practice

Use spectral_dim when topology or a weak boundary gives you a reason to look beyond the displayed coordinates. On the circle and COIL-20, a pair of modes completes a closed path. MNIST supplies a useful neighboring view, with less support in the added coordinate. Fashion-MNIST shows that a larger computed block can remain concentrated throughout.

Read the plots together with support and boundary gaps, after checking graph, rank, and solver diagnostics. Diagnosing suspicious LTSA results gives the returned fields and the action associated with each signal.

Retaining a block supplies candidate coordinates; choosing which coordinates to display is a separate problem. Independent Eigencoordinate Selection is one published method for selecting smooth, locally independent coordinates from a larger spectral set. spectral_dim does not perform that selection; it exposes the candidate modes needed to investigate it.

Trying It Yourself

Here’s a compact version of the COIL-20 example. Install flotsam, snedata, vizier 0.6.2 or later, and ggplot2:

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak(c(
  "jlmelville/flotsam", "jlmelville/snedata", "jlmelville/vizier", "ggplot2"
))

Download object 4 and retain four coordinates from the one-dimensional local model. The pose values are used only to color the plot.

coil <- snedata::download_coil20(as = "list")
rows <- coil$meta$object == 4L
X <- coil$data[rows, , drop = FALSE]
pose <- as.integer(as.character(coil$meta$pose[rows]))

fit <- flotsam::ltsa(
  X, ndim = 1, n_neighbors = 7, nn_method = "exact", eig_method = "eig",
  eig_k = 8, output = "result", spectral_dim = 4
)
vizier::embed_ggplot(
  fit$spectral_embedding[, 1:2], pose,
  color_scheme = grDevices::hcl.colors(256, "Dynamic"), num_colors = 256,
  fixed_aspect = TRUE, title = "COIL-20 object 4: modes 1 and 2"
)

Try fit$spectral_embedding[, 2:3] to inspect the next pair. The article figures add thumbnails of the object; this example plots the coordinates and pose colors.

Data Sources

The image examples use COIL-20 (Sameer A. Nene, Shree K. Nayar, and Hiroshi Murase), MNIST (Yann LeCun, Corinna Cortes, and Christopher J. C. Burges), and Fashion-MNIST (Han Xiao, Kashif Rasul, and Roland Vollgraf).
